pages.title: A second job: the lathe, start to finish
pages.for: One pass through a whole design. Work Ib at the board’s own voltage. Choose the device, then the cable for where it runs. Add every drop from the intake. Then choose the cpc. Table 54.7’s size needs no calculation. A smaller one is fine only when Zs and the heat check both pass.
pages.rule:
U at the board = U × (1 − the upstream drop)
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg). Ca is above 1 below 30 °C
Drop from the intake = upstream + mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000
Smaller cpc: Zs ≤ max Zs, and S ≥ √(I² × t) ÷ k at Cmax
Longest run = (max Zs − Zs at the board) × 1000 ÷ (mΩ/m × multiplier)
Armour: at least k1 ÷ k2 × S, with 16 for S above 16 mm², up to 35 mm²
Core and armour: R2 = 1 ÷ (1 ÷ Ra + 1 ÷ Rc)

Armour short? Use a cable with an extra core, or a separate cpc sized for the whole fault current.

traps.text: Checking only the heat when the cpc is cut. A thinner cpc raises Zs too.
traps.cite: Mock part 2 p.1 (ADS asked first); OSG Table I1 p.218

traps.text: Working the cpc’s heat at the Cmin current. While the breaker opens within 0.1 s, Cmax gives the larger area.
Calling Table 54.7’s size the minimum. It is the suitable size. Only a calculation gives the minimum.
traps.cite: Course flowchart note 2; NICEIC/ELECSA (Table 54.7 as an alternative to calculation)

traps.text: Passing a cpc by a hair, then finding it reads over the inspector’s cold limit. Work the expected reading and hand it over.
traps.cite: OSG p.139 and p.146; Voltimum (cold reading at most 80% of tabulated)

traps.text: Working Ib at 400 V when the board sits lower. Work it at the board’s own voltage: 388 V at DB2.
traps.cite: Mock part 1 p.1 (3% drop to DB2); slides p.13

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A motor circuit runs 27 m in 4 mm² singles with a 4 mm² cpc. Zs is 0.4 Ω at its board and 0.719 Ω at the motor. The client wants the cpc cut to 2.5 mm². Which checks must you work again?
pages.answer: Zs against the breaker's maximum, and the heat check
pages.why: R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 0.415 Ω. So Zs rises from 0.719 Ω to 0.815 Ω, which must stay within the breaker's maximum. The thinner cpc must still take the fault's heat. The cpc carries no load current, so the rating and the drop stay as they were.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
One whole job in one pass, on a circuit unlike the showroom's. A lathe motor is fed from a board that sits below 400 V. Its cable shares trunking with two other circuits.

Then a question every designer meets. Can the cpc be smaller than Table 54.7's size? Yes, if two checks still pass. Zs must stay within the breaker's maximum. And the cpc must take the fault's heat.
pages.alt: One whole job in one pass, on a circuit unlike the showroom's. A lathe motor is fed from a board that sits below 400 V. Its cable shares trunking with two other circuits. Then a question every designer meets. Can the cpc be smaller than Table 54.7's size? Yes, if two checks still pass. Zs must stay within the breaker's maximum. And the cpc must take the fault's heat. If Zs is not rechecked: Cut the cpc on the heat check alone and Zs can rise past the maximum. Then the breaker may not open in time.
pages.html:
One whole job in one pass, on a circuit unlike the showroom's. A lathe motor is fed from a board that sits below 400 V. Its cable shares trunking with two other circuits.

Then a question every designer meets. Can the cpc be smaller than Table 54.7's size? Yes, if two checks still pass. Zs must stay within the breaker's maximum. And the cpc must take the fault's heat.

If Zs is not rechecked: Cut the cpc on the heat check alone and Zs can rise past the maximum. Then the breaker may not open in time.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 27 m the 2.5 mm² cpc gives Zs 0.815 Ω, within 0.87 Ω. It needs only 0.69 mm² for the heat. The 1.5 mm² cpc gives 0.977 Ω and fails on Zs.
pages.alt: DB2 Zs 0.4 Ω Line 4 mm² cpc 2.5 mm² M Lathe 27 m The loop: Zs = 0.4 + 0.415 = 0.815 Ω At DB2 R1+R2 Max 0.87 Ω The heat: needs at least 0.69 mm² 2.5 mm² fitted Fault current at Cmin 268.10 A Needs 250 A or more Longest run, this cpc 30.5 m With a 2.5 mm² cpc over 27 m, Zs is 0.815 Ω, inside the 0.87 Ω line. The heat needs only 0.69 mm² of the 2.5 mm² fitted. Both checks pass. Zs = 0.4 + mΩ/m × 1.28 × length ÷ 1000. It must stay within 0.87 Ω. Least cpc = √(I² × 0.1) ÷ 143, with I = 253 ÷ Zs, the fault current at Cmax. A thinner cpc raises Zs. That eases the heat but tightens the loop.
pages.html:
Fault current at Cmin268.10 ANeeds 250 A or more
Longest run, this cpc30.5 m

With a 2.5 mm² cpc over 27 m, Zs is 0.815 Ω, inside the 0.87 Ω line. The heat needs only 0.69 mm² of the 2.5 mm² fitted. Both checks pass.

Zs = 0.4 + mΩ/m × 1.28 × length ÷ 1000. It must stay within 0.87 Ω.

Least cpc = √(I² × 0.1) ÷ 143, with I = 253 ÷ Zs, the fault current at Cmax.

A thinner cpc raises Zs. That eases the heat but tightens the loop. On the lathe the loop, not the heat, sets the smallest cpc.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: Keep the 2.5 mm² cpc. The lathe moves, and the run becomes 32 m. Is the circuit still acceptable?
pages.answer: No: Zs is 0.892 Ω, over 0.87 Ω
pages.why: R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 32 ÷ 1000 = 0.492 Ω. Zs = 0.4 + 0.492 = 0.892 Ω, over 0.87 Ω. The longest run with 2.5 mm² is 30.5 m. Go back to the 4 mm² cpc, good to 39.8 m.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: Both four-core cables have more armour than Table 54.7 asks. With the core and the armour in parallel, Zs is 0.101 Ω. Each path alone takes the heat.
pages.alt: STEEL ARMOUR AS THE CPC A 6 mm² four-core 90 °C SWA. Table 54.7 asks for k1 ÷ k2 × S of armour. Take k1 = 143 for the copper and k2 = 46 for the steel. 46 is a practice value. On a real job, check it in Table 54.4. Armour needed = 143 × 6 ÷ 46 = 18.65 mm² The cable has 36 mm² of armour. Enough. A 25 mm² four-core. Above 16 mm², up to 35 mm², Table 54.7 uses 16 in place of S. Armour needed = 143 × 16 ÷ 46 = 49.74 mm² The cable has 70 mm². Enough. Take armour areas from the maker's sheet for the cable you buy.
pages.html:
Steel armour as the cpc

A 6 mm² four-core 90 °C SWA. Table 54.7 asks for k1 ÷ k2 × S of armour. Take k1 = 143 for the copper and k2 = 46 for the steel. 46 is a practice value. On a real job, check it in Table 54.4.

Armour needed = 143 × 6 ÷ 46 = 18.65 mm²

The cable has 36 mm² of armour. Enough.

A 25 mm² four-core. Above 16 mm², up to 35 mm², Table 54.7 uses 16 in place of S.

Armour needed = 143 × 16 ÷ 46 = 49.74 mm²

The cable has 70 mm². Enough. Take armour areas from the maker's sheet for the cable you buy.

If it had fallen short, choose a cable with an extra core, or run a separate cpc alongside. A separate cpc must be sized for the whole fault current.

A 25 mm² five-core, 26 m, on a 40 A BS 88-2 fuse. Take Ze as 0.06 Ω. The fifth core and the armour share the cpc's job. Take 1.28 on the armour too. It runs cooler, so this errs safe.

R2 = 1 ÷ (1 ÷ 0.727 + 1 ÷ 1.8) = 0.518 mΩ/m

R1+R2 = (0.727 + 0.518) × 1.28 × 26 ÷ 1000 = 0.041 Ω

Zs = 0.06 + 0.041 = 0.101 Ω

Fault current at Cmax = 253 ÷ 0.101 = 2504.95 A

Work the heat at Cmax. It gives the larger area. Take 0.1 s for the fuse here, as a practice value. On a real job, read the time from Figure 3A3.

Armour alone: √(2504.95² × 0.1) ÷ 46 = 17.22 mm², within its 88 mm²

Core alone: √(2504.95² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 5.54 mm², within 25 mm²

Both pass.

pages.name: Section A 5(a)
pages.task: Use 0.4 Ω for Zs at DB2, even if you have 0.97 Ω written down. At 0.97 Ω no 25 A type C could pass. (a) Determine the design current of the lathe circuit.
pages.alt: The lathe at DB2 SCENARIO A workshop on a 400 V three-phase TN-C-S supply, Ze 0.12 Ω, prospective fault current 8 kA at the origin. DB2 is fed by a distribution circuit that drops 3%. Zs at DB2 is 0.4 Ω. From DB2, a circuit feeds a 12.5 kW three-phase lathe motor, power factor 0.91 and efficiency 94% at full load. It runs 27 m in 90 °C thermosetting singles in trunking on a wall, with two other loaded circuits, at 25 °C. Protection is a type C circuit-breaker to BS EN 60898. Use 0.4 Ω for Zs at DB2, even if you have 0.97 Ω written down. At 0.97 Ω no 25 A type C could pass.
pages.html:
The lathe at DB2Scenario

A workshop on a 400 V three-phase TN-C-S supply, Ze 0.12 Ω, prospective fault current 8 kA at the origin. DB2 is fed by a distribution circuit that drops 3%. Zs at DB2 is 0.4 Ω. From DB2, a circuit feeds a 12.5 kW three-phase lathe motor, power factor 0.91 and efficiency 94% at full load. It runs 27 m in 90 °C thermosetting singles in trunking on a wall, with two other loaded circuits, at 25 °C. Protection is a type C circuit-breaker to BS EN 60898.

Use 0.4 Ω for Zs at DB2, even if you have 0.97 Ω written down. At 0.97 Ω no 25 A type C could pass.

U at DB2 = 400 × 0.97 = 388.00 V

√3 × 388 = 672.04

× 0.91 = 611.56

× 0.94 = 574.87

Ib = 12 500 ÷ 574.87 = 21.74 A

pages.name: Section A 5(b) and (c)
pages.task: (b) The next standard rating above 21.74 A is 25 A, type C. Assume the lathe's terminals and the breaker allow the cable to run at 90 °C. Table 4B1 gives Ca 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting cable at 25 °C. It is above 1 because the tables are set at 30 °C. A cooler room takes heat away faster. Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits in the trunking. (c) Determine the minimum tabulated current-carrying capacity, It.
pages.alt: CARRIED FORWARD (a) The lathe's design current, Ib 21.74 A (b) The next standard rating above 21.74 A is 25 A, type C. Assume the lathe's terminals and the breaker allow the cable to run at 90 °C. Table 4B1 gives Ca 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting cable at 25 °C. It is above 1 because the tables are set at 30 °C. A cooler room takes heat away faster. Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits in the trunking. Give It in A, to two places. Factors together = 1.02 × 0.70 = 0.714 It = 25 ÷ 0.714 = 35.01 A (d) In Table 4E1A, column 5, for three loaded singles, 2.5 mm² gives 28 A. That is too small.

(a)The lathe's design current, Ib21.74 A

(b) The next standard rating above 21.74 A is 25 A, type C.

Assume the lathe's terminals and the breaker allow the cable to run at 90 °C.

Table 4B1 gives Ca 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting cable at 25 °C. It is above 1 because the tables are set at 30 °C. A cooler room takes heat away faster.

Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits in the trunking.

Give It in A, to two places.

Factors together = 1.02 × 0.70 = 0.714

It = 25 ÷ 0.714 = 35.01 A

(d) In Table 4E1A, column 5, for three loaded singles, 2.5 mm² gives 28 A. That is too small. 4 mm² gives 37 A. Iz = 37 × 0.714 = 26.42 A, at least 25 A. So 4 mm².

(f) Table 54.7: a copper cpc with a line of 16 mm² or less is the line's size, so 4 mm².

The client asks for a 2.5 mm² cpc to save copper.

Table I1 gives 12.02 mΩ/m for a 4 mm² line with a 2.5 mm² cpc. Table I3 gives 1.28 to bring it up to 90 °C.

Give Zs in Ω. Whether it complies follows.

R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 0.415 Ω

Zs = 0.4 + 0.415 = 0.815 Ω

0.815 Ω is within 0.87 Ω. At Cmin, 218.5 ÷ 0.815 = 268.10 A. That is past the 250 A that opens the breaker within 0.1 s. So it complies.

Table 54.3 gives k 143 for a copper cpc bunched with 90 °C thermosetting cables.

Give the area in mm², to two places. Whether it is adequate follows.

Fault current at Cmax = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.815 = 310.43 A

That is past 250 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s. Take t = 0.1 s.

k = 143 for a copper cpc bunched with 90 °C thermosetting cables.

S = √(310.43² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 0.69 mm²

0.69 mm² is well under 2.5 mm², so it is adequate. Both checks pass. The loop is the closer one, at 0.815 Ω against 0.87 Ω.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: The client asks for the lathe’s cpc to be cut to 2.5 mm² to save copper. Explain whether you would agree, and what the inspector must be told.
pages.why: A model answer: It complies, but I would advise against it. With a 2.5 mm² cpc, Zs at the lathe is 0.815 Ω, within the breaker’s 0.87 Ω. So 268.10 A flows at Cmin and opens it within 0.1 s. For the heat the cpc needs only 0.69 mm², so 2.5 mm² is enough. But the margin is thin. The run can be no longer than 30.5 m. Table 54.7’s 4 mm² is the suitable size. A smaller cpc stands only on this calculation. So I would keep 4 mm². If 2.5 mm² goes in, I would tell the inspector to expect about 0.725 Ω cold. That is over the 0.680 Ω rule of thumb, yet it passes. Only the circuit warms up. Zs at DB2 does not.

pages.html:
A 40 A BS 88-2 fuse-switch feeds a 63 A TP&N workshop board through a 26 m distribution circuit. After diversity it carries 32 A per phase. It is 70 °C thermoplastic singles in trunking with two other circuits, at 35 °C. The drop must not exceed 6 V. Table 4B1 gives Ca 0.94 at 35 °C. Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits.

Same method, new numbers. Give It in A, to two places.

Ca = 0.94 at 35 °C, Cg = 0.70

Factors together = 0.94 × 0.70 = 0.658

It = 40 ÷ 0.658 = 60.79 A

In Table 4D1A, column 5, 10 mm² gives 50 A. That is too small, so 16 mm² at 68 A. Its drop is 2.4 × 32 × 26 ÷ 1000 = 2.00 V, inside 6 V.

The board's 63 A rating is at least the 40 A fuse ahead of it, as Regulation 536.4.202 asks.
